newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam's president battles on despite stroke.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam's president battles on despite stroke.

text.p: Vietnam's President Le Duc Anh, one of the communist country's ruling triumvirate, lay in critical condition in a Hanoi hospital on Sunday after suffering a stroke, Vietnamese political sources said.
The 75-year-old army general regained consciousness and had already asked to be allowed to return to work.
But one of the sources, who declined to be named, said doctors were not optimistic that Anh would recover sufficiently to carry on as president.

Government officials earlier confirmed that Anh had been admitted to Hanoi's 108 Army hospital on Friday. But there have been widely varying reports of his condition since admission and an official veil of secrecy has been drawn across the situation.

One source said on Sunday evening that Anh had been paralysed down one side of his body by haemorrhaging around the brain. This was at odds with the comment of a medical worker earlier that his condition had improved and he might be discharged soon.
The hospital was barred to journalists, the official media made no mention of the president's condition and his aides and advisers could not be contacted by telephone.

State television, apparently reading from a Foreign Ministry news schedule issued several days ago, said Anh and his wife would be meeting South Korea's President Kim Young-sam during a visit later this week.
Hanoi's political rumour mill had been awash with speculation about the president's health over the past week because of several absences from public view.
The last activity reported by state media was his signing on Tuesday of a decision ratifying recent cabinet changes.

Anh is a key figure in the communist country's leadership triumvirate, a collective system comprising three powerful figures chosen to ensure balance between different shades of socialist opinion and differing regional views.
The other members of the trio are Communist Party chief Do Muoi, 79, seen as occupying a central and stabilising role in government, and reformist Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet, 73.

Anh, viewed by Western observers as the most conservative of the three, played key roles in independence struggles against the French and then the Americans, in the 1978 invasion of Cambodia and, finally, in normalising relations with China in 1991.
As president, he is also seen as an essential part of the mechanism by which close party-army ties are ensured.
Diplomats say the impact of his possible departure from the political scene would depend largely on the choice of successor.
The next most senior member of the elite Politburo below Anh, and with a military background, is Lieutenant-General Le Kha Phieu, 64.
